notes.definition: Selective breeding (artificial selection) is the process by which humans breed plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics, by choosing which individuals are allowed to reproduce.
explanation: Humans have been selectively breeding plants and animals for thousands of years, ever since they first bred food crops from wild plants and domesticated wild animals. Modern wheat, for example, has much larger grains than its wild grass ancestors, and all breeds of domestic dog are descended from wolves. Selective breeding is also called artificial selection because humans, rather than the environment, decide which individuals reproduce.

The process has four main stages. First, choose parents with the desired characteristic from a mixed population. Second, breed them together. Third, from the offspring, choose those with the desired characteristic and breed them together. Fourth, continue this over many generations until all the offspring show the desired characteristic. Because it relies on the natural variation already present and only one generation can be produced at a time, selective breeding usually takes many years.

The characteristic chosen can be for usefulness or for appearance. Examples include disease resistance in food crops, animals that produce more meat or milk, domestic dogs with a gentle nature, and large or unusual flowers. Farmers have bred cattle that give far more milk than their ancestors, wheat plants with short stems that do not fall over in the wind, and crops that ripen at the same time so they can be harvested easily.

Selective breeding has had a major impact on food plants and domesticated animals. It has greatly increased food production, making crops higher yielding and livestock more productive, and it has produced pets and garden plants with characteristics people value. However, because only a few individuals with the chosen trait are bred, selective breeding reduces the variety of alleles in the population. This can lead to inbreeding, where closely related individuals are bred together.

Inbreeding means some breeds are particularly prone to disease or inherited defects. Harmful recessive alleles are more likely to be inherited from both related parents, so offspring are more likely to show the disorder; for example, some pedigree dog breeds commonly suffer from joint or breathing problems. A population with little variation is also at risk if a new disease appears or the environment changes: if no individuals carry alleles for resistance, the whole population could be affected, and there is less variation for future breeding.
keyFacts: Selective breeding (artificial selection) is humans breeding plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics.
Humans have done this for thousands of years, since first breeding crops from wild plants and domesticating animals.
Choose parents with the desired characteristic from a mixed population and breed them.
Choose offspring with the desired characteristic and breed them together.
Repeat over many generations until all offspring show the characteristic.
Characteristics can be chosen for usefulness or appearance.
Examples: disease-resistant crops, more meat or milk, gentle dogs, large or unusual flowers.
Selective breeding can lead to inbreeding, making some breeds prone to disease or inherited defects.
It reduces variation (the range of alleles) in a population.

keyTerms.definition: Humans choosing which plants or animals reproduce in order to produce offspring with particular genetic characteristics. Also called artificial selection.
Another name for selective breeding: humans, not the environment, select which individuals breed.
The trait a breeder wants, such as high milk yield, disease resistance or a gentle nature.
Breeding between closely related individuals, which increases the chance of offspring inheriting two copies of a harmful recessive allele.
A health problem caused by alleles passed on from the parents.
An animal that has been bred by humans over many generations to live with or be used by people, such as cattle, sheep and dogs.
Differences in characteristics between individuals; selective breeding reduces genetic variation in a breed.

workedExamples.title: Describing the method
workedExamples.question: A farmer wants to produce a herd of sheep with thicker wool. Describe how she could use selective breeding.
steps: From her mixed flock, choose a ram and ewes with the thickest wool.
From the lambs, choose those with the thickest wool when they mature and breed them together.
Repeat for many generations until all the offspring have thick wool.
workedExamples.answer: Select parents with thick wool, breed them, select the best offspring, breed those, and repeat over many generations.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a percentage increase
workedExamples.question: In 1960 the average milk yield of a herd was 3500 litres per cow per year. After selective breeding it rose to 8400 litres. Calculate the percentage increase.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a disadvantage
workedExamples.question: Explain why a crop variety produced by selective breeding could be wiped out by a new disease.
steps: Selective breeding uses only a few parents, so the variety has little genetic variation.
The plants have very similar alleles.
If none carries an allele for resistance to the new disease, all are susceptible.
workedExamples.answer: Low genetic variation means there may be no resistant plants, so the whole crop could be killed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think selective breeding creates new genes or new alleles.
misconceptions.right: In fact selective breeding only uses alleles that already exist in the population; it changes how common they are. Genetic engineering is the technique that introduces genes from another organism.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think selective breeding gives the desired result in one generation.
misconceptions.right: In fact it takes many generations of selecting and breeding before all the offspring show the desired characteristic.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse selective breeding with natural selection.
misconceptions.right: In fact in selective breeding humans choose which individuals breed; in natural selection the environment determines which individuals survive to breed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think selectively bred organisms are always healthier.
misconceptions.right: In fact inbreeding means some breeds are particularly prone to disease or inherited defects, and low variation makes them vulnerable to new diseases.

realWorld: Modern dairy cattle such as Holsteins have been bred to produce several times more milk per year than cattle did a century ago.
Wild mustard has been selectively bred into several vegetables, including cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts, by choosing different parts of the plant.
Short-stemmed, high-yield wheat varieties bred in the twentieth century greatly increased world food production.
Some pedigree dog breeds, such as pugs and bulldogs, often have breathing problems because of their selectively bred flat faces and inbreeding.
examTips: When describing selective breeding, include all the stages: choose parents with the characteristic, breed, choose the best offspring, breed them, repeat over many generations.
Always use the phrase 'many generations'; it is a common mark point.
For disadvantages, name inbreeding and link it to inherited defects or disease, and mention reduced variation.
If asked to compare with genetic engineering, say selective breeding is slower and only uses existing alleles within a species.
In 'explain the impact' questions give both benefits (more food, useful or attractive traits) and problems (inbreeding, less variation).
summary: Selective breeding is humans breeding organisms for particular genetic characteristics.
It has been done for thousands of years to produce crops and domesticated animals.
Choose parents with the desired trait, breed them, select the best offspring and repeat for many generations.
Traits are chosen for usefulness (disease resistance, more meat or milk) or appearance (flowers, gentle dogs).
It reduces genetic variation and can lead to inbreeding.
Inbred breeds can be prone to disease and inherited defects.

questions.question: What is another name for selective breeding?
options: Natural selection
Artificial selection
Genetic engineering
Cloning
markScheme: 1 mark: artificial selection
questions.explanation: Selective breeding is artificial selection because humans choose which organisms breed. Natural selection is driven by the environment; genetic engineering and cloning are different techniques.

questions.question: Which characteristic might a farmer selectively breed dairy cattle for?
options: High milk yield
Brightly coloured flowers
Resistance to herbicides
Gentle nature in sheepdogs
markScheme: 1 mark: high milk yield
questions.explanation: Dairy cattle are bred to produce more milk. Flowers are plants, herbicide resistance in crops is usually produced by genetic engineering, and sheepdogs are not cattle.

questions.question: What is the first step in selective breeding?
options: Insert a gene from another species
Take cuttings from a plant
Choose parents with the desired characteristic
Wait for a mutation to occur
markScheme: 1 mark: choose parents with the desired characteristic
questions.explanation: Selective breeding starts by choosing parents from a mixed population that show the desired characteristic. Inserting genes is genetic engineering; taking cuttings is cloning.

questions.question: What problem can be caused by inbreeding?
options: Offspring are always infertile
Increased genetic variation
A new species forms immediately
An increased chance of inherited defects
markScheme: 1 mark: an increased chance of inherited defects
questions.explanation: Inbreeding makes some breeds particularly prone to disease and inherited defects. It reduces variation rather than increasing it, and it does not make offspring infertile or create new species.

questions.question: Why does selective breeding usually take many years?
options: The desired gene must be cut out with enzymes
Selection and breeding must be repeated over many generations
Animals must first be cloned
Mutations must be caused deliberately
markScheme: 1 mark: selection and breeding repeated over many generations
questions.explanation: Each round of selection needs a new generation to grow up and breed, and many rounds are needed before all offspring show the trait. Cutting genes with enzymes is genetic engineering.

questions.question: Which statement about selective breeding is correct?
options: It introduces genes from a different species
It only works in plants
It uses variation that already exists within a species
It increases the genetic variation in a breed
markScheme: 1 mark: it uses variation that already exists within a species
questions.explanation: Breeders select from alleles already present. Introducing genes from another species is genetic engineering. Selective breeding is used for both plants and animals and reduces variation.

questions.question: A plant breeder crosses two wheat plants. Which pair would be the best choice to produce a variety with high yield and disease resistance?
options: A high-yield plant and a disease-resistant plant
Two low-yield plants
Two plants that are both easily diseased
A disease-resistant plant and a short-lived plant
markScheme: 1 mark: a high-yield plant and a disease-resistant plant
questions.explanation: To combine two characteristics, breed parents that each have one of them, then select offspring with both over several generations.

questions.question: Why are inbred animals more likely to show inherited disorders?
options: Inbreeding causes mutations
Related parents are more likely to carry the same harmful recessive allele, so offspring may inherit two copies
Inbred animals have extra chromosomes
The environment of inbred animals is worse
markScheme: 1 mark: related parents likely to carry the same harmful recessive allele; offspring may get two copies
questions.explanation: Close relatives share many alleles. If both carry a harmful recessive allele, a quarter of their offspring could be homozygous and show the disorder. Inbreeding does not cause mutations or change chromosome number.

questions.question: All the banana plants on a large plantation belong to one selectively bred variety. Which is the greatest risk?
options: The bananas will become too large
The plants will evolve into a new species
A new disease could infect all plants because there is little genetic variation
The plants will start producing seeds
markScheme: 1 mark: a new disease could affect all plants because of low variation
questions.explanation: With little variation, if one plant is susceptible to a disease, they all probably are. No plants carry resistant alleles to survive and breed.

questions.question: A breed of hen laid 150 eggs per year. After selective breeding, hens of the new variety lay 300 eggs per year. How many more eggs per year does each hen lay?
markScheme: 1 mark: 150
questions.explanation: 300 − 150 = 150 more eggs per hen per year.

questions.question: The mean yield of a tomato variety was 4.0 kg per plant. After several generations of selective breeding it was 5.2 kg per plant. Calculate the percentage increase in yield.
markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 5.2 − 4.0 = 1.2 kg
questions.explanation: Percentage increase = increase ÷ original × 100 = 1.2 ÷ 4.0 × 100 = 30%.

questions.question: A breeder selects dogs for a gentle nature. A new generation is produced every 2 years. How many generations can be produced in 30 years?
markScheme: 1 mark: 30 ÷ 2
1 mark: = 15
questions.explanation: Number of generations = 30 ÷ 2 = 15. This shows why selective breeding of animals is a slow process.

questions.question: The average milk yield of a herd increased from 4200 litres to 9450 litres per cow per year over 35 years. Calculate the mean increase in yield per year.
markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 9450 − 4200 = 5250 litres
1 mark: 5250 ÷ 35 = 150 litres per year
questions.explanation: Total increase 5250 litres, divided over 35 years gives 150 litres per cow each year.

questions.question: In one generation, 120 of 480 young cattle showed resistance to a disease. Calculate the percentage that were NOT resistant.
markScheme: 1 mark: 120 ÷ 480 × 100 = 25% resistant
1 mark: 100 − 25 = 75(%) not resistant
questions.explanation: Resistant = 120 ÷ 480 = 0.25 = 25%. Not resistant = 75%. Alternatively, 360 ÷ 480 × 100 = 75%.

questions.question: Give one example of a characteristic that plants are selectively bred for.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one, e.g. disease resistance, high yield, large or unusual flowers, bigger fruit, taste
questions.explanation: Plants are bred for useful traits such as disease resistance and yield, or for appearance such as large or unusual flowers.

questions.question: State what is meant by inbreeding.
markScheme: 1 mark: breeding (mating) closely related individuals together
questions.explanation: Inbreeding happens when the only individuals with the desired trait are close relatives, so they are bred together.

questions.question: Give one reason why a dog breeder might selectively breed dogs.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one, e.g. gentle nature, appearance (size, coat), working ability
questions.explanation: Dogs are bred for nature (gentleness), appearance or usefulness, such as herding or guiding.

questions.question: Describe how a farmer could selectively breed pigs to produce more meat.
markScheme: 1 mark: choose (male and female) pigs that produce the most meat and breed them together
1 mark: select the offspring that produce the most meat and breed them together
1 mark: repeat over many generations (until all offspring produce more meat)
questions.explanation: The method has a selection stage, a breeding stage and repetition over many generations.

questions.question: Give two benefits of selective breeding for food production.
markScheme: 1 mark each for two benefits, e.g. higher crop yields, more meat or milk from animals, disease-resistant crops (less crop loss), better quality food (max 2)
questions.explanation: Selective breeding has greatly increased the amount of food produced from crops and livestock.

questions.question: Explain why selectively bred populations have less genetic variation than wild populations.
acceptedAnswers: only those with desired trait bred
markScheme: 1 mark: only a few individuals with the desired characteristic are chosen to breed
1 mark: so alleles in the other individuals are not passed on/are lost from the population
questions.explanation: Repeatedly breeding from a small selected group narrows the range of alleles in each generation.

questions.question: Compare selective breeding with natural selection. Give one similarity and one difference.
acceptedAnswers: both change allele frequency over generations
markScheme: 1 mark: similarity, e.g. both act on existing genetic variation / both change a population over many generations
1 mark: difference: in selective breeding humans choose which individuals breed, in natural selection the environment determines which survive to breed
questions.explanation: Both are selection processes acting on inherited variation over generations; the difference is who or what does the selecting.

questions.question: A rare breed of cattle has a very small population. Suggest why breeders are keen to keep this breed rather than replace it with a modern high-yield breed.
markScheme: 1 mark: modern breeds have low genetic variation (due to selective breeding/inbreeding)
1 mark: the rare breed may carry useful alleles, e.g. for disease resistance or hardiness
1 mark: these alleles could be used in future breeding programmes / protect against new diseases or environmental change
questions.explanation: Keeping varied breeds keeps a store of alleles that selective breeding has removed from commercial breeds.

questions.question: Wild cabbage was selectively bred to produce both broccoli and Brussels sprouts. Explain how one wild species could give rise to such different vegetables.
markScheme: 1 mark: the wild cabbage population showed variation in different features (e.g. flower heads, side buds)
1 mark: different breeders selected for different characteristics over many generations (large flower heads for broccoli, large buds for Brussels sprouts)
questions.explanation: Selecting for different traits from the same varied population, repeated over many generations, produces very different varieties.

questions.question: Some flat-faced dog breeds have breathing difficulties. Some people think breeding these dogs is unethical. Give one argument for this view and one argument against it.
markScheme: 1 mark: for: breeding for appearance causes suffering/inherited health problems to the animals
1 mark: against: e.g. people value these pets and responsible breeders can select healthier individuals / outcross to improve health
questions.explanation: Ethical questions need a balanced answer, with a reason for each side.

questions.question: A plant breeder wants a variety of strawberry that produces large fruit and is resistant to a fungal disease. Describe how she could use selective breeding to produce this variety.
markScheme: Indicative content: choose a parent plant with large fruit and a parent plant resistant to the fungus (from a mixed population); cross-pollinate (breed) them; grow the seeds; select offspring with both large fruit and disease resistance (test by exposing to the fungus); breed these together; repeat over many generations until all offspring have both characteristics.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear, ordered method including selection of parents with each trait, selection of offspring with both, and repetition over many generations.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'breed the best plants together' without a clear sequence.
questions.explanation: The plan should combine the two traits, select offspring that have both, and repeat over many generations.

questions.question: Explain the impact of selective breeding on food plants and domesticated animals. Include both benefits and problems.
markScheme: Indicative content. Benefits: humans have bred crops from wild plants and domesticated animals for thousands of years; increased crop yields; disease-resistant crops reduce losses and need for pesticides; animals produce more meat or milk; better quality, taste or appearance; animals with gentle nature easier to keep; helps feed a growing population. Problems: reduced genetic variation; inbreeding; some breeds particularly prone to disease or inherited defects (e.g. joint or breathing problems in dogs, health problems in high-yield cattle); low variation means a new disease or environmental change could affect the whole population; fewer alleles available for future breeding; animal welfare concerns.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed explanation with several benefits and several problems, linking reduced variation to inbreeding, inherited defects and vulnerability to disease, with examples.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes some benefits and at least one problem with some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements of benefits or problems with little explanation.
questions.explanation: A balanced answer explains why food production has risen and then explains the genetic cost: less variation, inbreeding, inherited defects and vulnerability to new diseases.
